legend.title: Color legend
leg.extra.pyraminx: The letters in algorithms are the vertices: U (top), L (left), R (right), B (back). Capital = turn the whole layer, lowercase = turn only the tip.
leg.extra.skewb: The letters are the corners that turn: R = bottom-right-front, L = top-left-front, U = top-right-back, B = bottom-left-back.
leg.extra.cube: The letters in algorithms are faces: R U F L D B (right, up, front, left, down, back).

ph.c0: no corner facing yellow up yet
tt.vls00: VLS · Corner and edge both in the last layer (324)
tt.vls10: VLS · Corner in the slot, edge in the last layer (81)
tt.vls01: VLS · Edge in the slot, corner in the last layer (81)
tt.vls11: VLS · Both in the slot, misaligned (16)
ph.vls00: This group has 324 cases where both the corner and the edge of the last pair are still in the last layer (not yet in the slot).
ph.vls10: This group has 81 cases where the corner is already in the slot and the edge is still in the last layer.
ph.vls01: This group has 81 cases where the edge is already in the slot and the corner is still in the last layer.
ph.vls11: This group has 16 cases where both the corner and the edge are in the slot but misaligned (wrongly paired).
t.vls:
VLS solves the last F2L pair and orients all 4 last-layer corners at the same time – like CLS, but only when the 4 last-layer edges are already oriented. {sub}
Pick the case that matches the positions of the corner and edge of the last pair. After VLS only COLL or PLL remains; with luck you finish right away.
t.ollcp:
OLLCP (OLL + Corner Permutation) makes the whole top face yellow and also puts the 4 last-layer corners in the right relative positions, so what remains is a simple PLL (edges only) or nothing at all.
This group: {edges}; {corners}. How to use it: like OLL, but also look at the corner positions to pick the case. After the algorithm the edges may still be misplaced – finish with EPLL (Ua, Ub, H or Z), or nothing if it is already solved.
t.zbll:
ZBLL (Zborowski–Bruchem Last Layer) solves the whole last layer with a single algorithm when the 4 last-layer edges are already oriented (yellow cross) – corner orientation, corner permutation and edge permutation in one go.
This group: {corners}. These are the most used cases after EO or whenever the top face already shows a yellow cross. Pick the case from the positions of the corners and edges seen from above.
t.1lll:
1LLL (One-Look Last Layer) solves the entire last layer – edge orientation, corner orientation, corner permutation and edge permutation – with one algorithm, from any last-layer situation. It is the largest set in the app, meant for deep practice.
This group: {edges}; {corners}. Look at the picture to identify the case, turn the top face (U) until it matches the pattern, then execute the algorithm.
n1: R – turn the right face clockwise
n9: Insert a corner into the first layer (repeat 1–5 times)
n10: Repeat until the corner is in the right place.
n12: Twist a corner that is already in place (repeat for each corner)
n13: Repeat 2 or 4 times for one corner, then turn the bottom layer to work on the next corner.
c14: OLL – make the top face yellow
c18: CLL · Top face already yellow (corner permutation only)
lv23: Optimal – shorten the last slot and the last layer
lv25: Roux branch – the alternative method: build 1×2×3 blocks, then solve the remaining corners and edges
lv27: Competition – the big sets that finish the last layer with one algorithm
n29: Two white edges next to each other (for example front and right) are swapped.
n31: Two white edges opposite each other (for example front and back) are swapped.
lv36: Basic – reduction method: centers → edges → 3x3 → parity
n42: r – another way to write Rw
n44: 2R – turn only the 2nd layer from the right
n45: 2U – turn only the 2nd layer from the top
n52: Flip an edge while pairing (last edge)
n53: Used when pairing edges with the reduction method. Keep the edge to flip at the front-right position.
n55: OLL parity – one edge is flipped
n56: Appears when the last layer has an odd number of flipped edges – impossible on a 3x3.
n57: PLL parity – two opposite edges are swapped
n58: PLL parity – two adjacent edges are swapped
lv60: Advanced – finish the last 2 centers and 2 edges quickly
n61: R – turn the outermost right layer
n63: 2R – turn only the 2nd layer from the right
n68: Commutator [A, B]: repeat to put the centers in place step by step.

d.2x2.notation:
Notation tells you which face turns and in which direction. A 2x2 only needs 3 faces – R (right), U (up) and F (front) – because the opposite faces give the same result (only the viewing direction differs).
A single letter = a 90° turn clockwise when looking straight at that face. An apostrophe (') = counterclockwise. A 2 = a 180° (half) turn.
d.2x2.begin:
Simple algorithms for beginners: insert and twist the corners of the first layer (usually the white layer) with the layer-by-layer method.
Place the corner you want to solve above the front-right slot, then repeat the algorithm until the corner sits in the right place with the right colors. Repeating up to 5 times brings a corner home (6 times returns the puzzle to where it started), so stop as soon as the corner is correct.
d.2x2.oll:
2x2 OLL makes the whole top face one color (all 4 corners oriented), whether or not the corners are in the right places yet.
There are 5 cases named after their shape: Sune, Anti-Sune, H, Pi and U. In the pictures a yellow sticker is already oriented. Turn the top face (U) until the picture matches (for Sune: one yellow sticker at the top-left corner), then execute the algorithm.
d.2x2.pbl:
PBL (Permute Both Layers) is the last step: after the top face is one color, put the corners in the right places in both layers.
Look for “headlights” (two adjacent corners with the same side color). If two adjacent corners are swapped use the adjacent-swap algorithm (Jb); if two diagonal corners are swapped use the diagonal-swap algorithm (Y). After the algorithm, turn the top face (U) to align.
d.2x2.cll-4:
CLL (Corners of the Last Layer) for 2x2 solves the whole last layer (orientation and permutation of the 4 corners) with a single algorithm, skipping separate OLL and PBL steps.
This group is for when the top face already has 4 yellow stickers (oriented) and only the corners need permuting. There are 2 short, easy-to-remember cases.
d.2x2.cll-1:
CLL (Corners of the Last Layer) for 2x2 solves the whole last layer (orientation and permutation of the 4 corners) with a single algorithm.
This group is for when the top face has only 1 yellow sticker (the Sune and Anti-Sune families), 12 cases. Look at the orientation of the other 3 corners and the side colors to choose the case.
d.2x2.cll-2:
CLL (Corners of the Last Layer) for 2x2 solves the whole last layer (orientation and permutation of the 4 corners) with a single algorithm.
This group is for when the top face has 2 yellow stickers (the T, U and L families), 18 cases. The two yellow stickers may be adjacent or diagonal – identify that first, then compare with the pictures.
d.2x2.cll-0:
CLL (Corners of the Last Layer) for 2x2 solves the whole last layer (orientation and permutation of the 4 corners) with a single algorithm.
This group is for when the top face has no yellow sticker at all (the H and Pi families), 10 cases. These are the hardest to recognize, so look carefully at the side colors.
d.3x3.cross:
The cross is the first step of CFOP: place the 4 white edges around the white center on the bottom so that each edge matches the center of its side face.
This section only has 2 “almost done” situations: the 4 white edges are in the bottom layer but two of them are swapped relative to the centers. Hold the cross at the bottom, turn the bottom layer until at least two edges match, then choose the algorithm by whether the two wrong edges are adjacent or opposite.
When you are learning you can build the cross intuitively; these algorithms are only a quick fix for the end.
d.3x3.f2l:
F2L (First Two Layers) solves the first and second layers at the same time: pair a white corner with its matching middle-layer edge, then insert the pair into the empty slot between two centers. Repeat 4 times for the 4 slots.
There are 41 cases grouped by where the pair is: Free Pairs, Connected Pairs, Disconnected Pairs, Corner In Slot, Edge In Slot and Pieces In Slot.
The pictures show the pair to solve in the front-right slot. For another slot, rotate the whole cube around y to bring that slot to the front-right and use the same algorithm.
Tip: understand how the pair moves instead of memorizing every move – many cases are variations of R U R' or U R U' R'.
d.3x3.oll:
OLL (Orientation of the Last Layer) makes all 9 stickers of the top face (the last layer) one color – usually yellow – without caring whether the pieces are in the right places yet.
There are 57 cases grouped by the shape of the yellow stickers seen from above: Dot, Line, L, T, Square, Fish, Knight Move, Awkward, Lightning, P, W, C, and the OCLL / All Corners group (edges already yellow, only corners left).
In the pictures a yellow sticker is already oriented and a gray one needs fixing; the small strips around the border show which side faces the yellow stickers are on.
How to use it: rotate the cube with yellow on top, turn the top face (U) until the picture matches, then execute the algorithm.
d.3x3.pll:
PLL (Permutation of the Last Layer) is the last step of CFOP: the top face is one color but the last-layer pieces are in the wrong places; the algorithm swaps them home without breaking the yellow face.
There are 21 cases: 3 that only permute corners (Aa, Ab, E), 4 that only permute edges (Ua, Ub, H, Z) and 14 that permute both corners and edges (T, Y, J, R, F, G, V, N…).
The pictures show the real colors of the top row of each side face. Look for “headlights” (two same-colored stickers next to each other on a face): how many there are and where they sit tells you the case.
After the algorithm, turn the top face (U) once more to align and finish the cube.
d.3x3.af2l:
Advanced F2L has 54 difficult or rare F2L situations, usually when the corner–edge pair is stuck or both pieces are in awkward places. With basic CFOP you solve each pair intuitively; here you learn algorithms that solve those cases in a short sequence.
The cases are grouped into Trapped Corner / Trapped Edge (a corner or edge is stuck) and the group where both pieces are in awkward places (Both Pieces).
How to use it: find the case that matches your situation, click it to see the cube, then press ▶ to watch each move. The algorithm finishes the slot while keeping the cross and the slots you already solved.
d.3x3.wv:
Winter Variation (WV) solves the last F2L pair and at the same time orients the 4 corners of the last layer (all four yellow stickers facing up), provided the last-layer edges are already oriented.
When it applies: the last pair is already connected (corner and edge stuck together) and the last-layer edges are oriented. WV is a subset of VLS.
After the algorithm only COLL or PLL remains, so you skip the OLL step. There are 27 cases.
d.3x3.sv:
Summer Variation (SV) is the “sibling” of Winter Variation: it solves the last F2L pair and orients the 4 last-layer corners at the same time, but for pairs that are separated or need an R U R'-style insertion, provided the last-layer edges are already oriented.
There are 27 cases. After the algorithm only COLL or PLL remains. Compare the position of the last pair in the picture with your cube to choose the case.
d.3x3.cls:
CLS (Corners Last Slot) solves the last F2L pair and also deals with the 4 last-layer corners, when the last-layer edges are already oriented. It extends Winter Variation with more cases: besides orienting corners, the algorithm arranges them so that the rest of the last layer is as short as possible.
There are 97 cases named “CLS FDR…” (FDR is the last slot at the front-right position). Some cases carry the labels Trapped (a stuck piece) or Cross Color (related to the cross color).
After CLS you only have ELL (edges) or a short PLL left, which makes this an important optimization between F2L and the last layer.
d.3x3.coll:
COLL (Corners of the Last Layer) solves all 4 last-layer corners (orientation and position) in one algorithm, when the 4 last-layer edges are already oriented (the top face already has a yellow cross).
There are 40 cases grouped by corner shape: Sune, Anti Sune, T, Pi, H and other OCLL cases. After COLL only EPLL (Ua, Ub, H or Z) remains, or nothing if the edges are solved too.
It greatly shortens the solve compared with OLL + PLL and raises the chance of skipping the last step.
d.3x3.ell:
ELL (Edges of the Last Layer) solves only the 4 last-layer edges while the 4 last-layer corners have already been solved (for example after CLS or CMLL).
There are 25 cases grouped by how many edges are flipped (0, 2 or 4) and how they are permuted: the “4 Flip” cases have all 4 edges flipped; the others have edges misplaced, misoriented or both.
Each algorithm orients and permutes the edges at the same time, taking the last layer to the solved state.
d.3x3.antipll:
Anti PLL is a special subset of ELL: the 4 last-layer corners are already solved but all 4 edges are flipped, so the top face shows only the corners in yellow.
Each of the 22 cases is a permutation of the edges (named after PLL: Aa, Ab, E, F, Ga, Gb, H, Ua, Ub, Z…) combined with flipping all 4 edges. Recognize it by the orientation of the edge stickers on the top face, then pick the algorithm with the matching name.
d.3x3.sbls:
SBLS (Second Block Last Slot) is the second step of the Roux method: once the left 1×2×3 block is built, you finish the right 1×2×3 block by inserting the last pair into the remaining slot while keeping the left block intact.
There are 65 cases named after the position of the edge (for example “U UF” means the edge is at the UF position of the top layer); some have a “Corner on” label that tells where the corner is. Find the positions of the corner and edge of the last pair and choose the matching case.
d.3x3.cmll:
CMLL (Corners of the Last Layer) is the third step of Roux: with both 1×2×3 blocks built, you solve the 4 last-layer corners (orientation and position) with one algorithm, ignoring the remaining edges.
There are 42 cases grouped by corner orientation: O (all 4 oriented), Sune, Anti-Sune, H, Pi, U, T, L. The algorithms do not break the two 1×2×3 blocks. After CMLL you move on to LSE to solve the 6 remaining edges.
d.3x3.eo4a:
EO4a is the first step of LSE (Last Six Edges) in Roux: with both 1×2×3 blocks and the 4 last-layer corners done, only 6 edges remain (the 4 top edges and the 2 edges in the bottom middle row). These algorithms orient (flip into the right orientation) the wrong edges, mostly with M and U moves.
There are 9 cases; the names tell you how many edges are misoriented and where (for example “All 6” is all six edges, “4 Top” is the four top edges…). After orienting the edges you continue by solving the remaining edges.
d.4x4.notation:
Big cubes (4x4 and 5x5) have several layers, so the notation adds ways to choose layers.
Lowercase letters (r, u, f…) or capital letters followed by w (Rw, Uw…) = turn the 2 outermost layers together toward that side. A number in front (2R, 2U…) = turn only the n-th layer counted from that face. An apostrophe (') = counterclockwise, a 2 at the end = half turn. The letters x, y, z = rotate the whole cube around that axis.
d.4x4.centers:
Reduction method: first build the 6 centers (4 pieces each), then pair the edges, and finally solve it like a 3x3.
These algorithms only swap center pieces and do not affect corners and edges, so you can use them at any time while building centers. Rotate the whole cube to bring the two center pieces you want to swap to the positions the algorithm asks for, and repeat until all 6 centers have the right color.
d.4x4.edges:
After the centers, the next step is edge pairing: each edge of a 3x3 is made of 2 pieces on a 4x4 that must be joined.
This algorithm flips an edge when the last pair is in the wrong orientation, helping you finish the last edge of the pairing step. Once all 12 edges are paired the cube becomes a “big 3x3” and can be solved with CFOP or any layer method.
d.4x4.parity:
Parity is a situation that only appears on even-sized cubes (4x4): after solving it like a 3x3 you may reach a state a real 3x3 can never have.
OLL parity: one edge is flipped in the last layer. PLL parity: two edges are swapped (adjacent or opposite). Use the matching algorithm to fix it, then keep solving as a normal 3x3. These algorithms are long, so watch them move by move and practice a lot.
d.4x4.ollparity:
OLL parity happens when the last layer has an odd number of flipped edges – impossible on a 3x3. Sign: only 1 or 3 edges are flipped on the last face instead of an even number.
There are 3 variants: Basic (the standard algorithm), Pure (uses only inner layers, no x rotation) and M (adds M for a more comfortable fingertrick). Use whichever feels best, then continue with OLL/PLL.
d.4x4.pllparity:
PLL parity happens when two edges of the last layer are swapped while the corners are already correct – impossible on a 3x3. Sign: after OLL, two edges need swapping in a way no 3x3 PLL can do.
There are 22 cases: the parity algorithm is combined with the PLL, so you fix the parity and finish the PLL in one step. Choose the case that matches the PLL you have.
d.5x5.notation:
A 5x5 has 5 layers and fixed centers, so there is no parity like on a 4x4. The notation extends to the inner layers.
Lowercase letters (r, u…) or capitals followed by w (Rw, Uw…) = turn the 2 outer layers; 3Rw = turn the 3 outer layers. A number in front (2R, 3R…) = turn only the n-th layer from that face (3R is the middle layer). An apostrophe (') = counterclockwise, a 2 at the end = half turn. The letters x, y, z = rotate the whole cube.
d.5x5.centers:
Reduction method: build the centers first (9 pieces each on a 5x5), then pair the edges, then solve like a 3x3.
These algorithms only swap center pieces and do not affect corners and edges. There are 2 kinds: a 3-center cycle (a commutator you repeat to fill the centers step by step) and swaps of 4 or 6 center pieces using half turns. Put the two pieces you want to swap in the right positions, run the algorithm and repeat until all 6 centers have the right color.
d.5x5.edges:
After the centers, pair the edges: each edge of a 3x3 is made of 3 pieces on a 5x5 that must be joined.
There are 2 main algorithms: one flips an edge when pairing the last pair, the other brings an edge up from the middle layer to pair it. A 5x5 has no parity, so once the 12 edges are paired you can solve it right away like a 3x3.
d.5x5.l2c:
L2C (Last Two Centers) completes the last 2 centers of a 5x5 with one algorithm, once the other 4 centers are done. It is an optimization that saves you from repeating a manual algorithm many times.
There are 18 cases, depending on how the center pieces of the two remaining faces are mixed. Find the position of the wrong pieces and pick the matching case.
d.5x5.l2e:
L2E (Last Two Edges) pairs the last 2 edges of a 5x5 with one algorithm, once the other 10 edges are paired. It is an optimization that saves you from repeating the manual edge-pairing algorithms.
There are 13 cases, depending on the positions of the 4 remaining edge pieces. The algorithms use inner layers (3Rw, Lw…), so pay attention to every symbol.
d.pyraminx.notation:
A Pyraminx has 4 vertices (axes) and every axis turns independently. The letters in an algorithm are the names of the vertices: U (top), L (left), R (right), B (back).
Capital letters (U, L, R, B) = turn the whole layer around that vertex (the small tip plus the middle layer, i.e. 2/3 of the puzzle). Lowercase letters (u, l, r, b) = turn only the small tip. Clockwise is taken when looking straight at the vertex; an apostrophe (') = counterclockwise. Each turn is 120°.
d.pyraminx.edges:
A Pyraminx has 6 edges. After the 4 tips and 4 axes are in place, you need to bring the 6 edges home. These algorithms only change edges and keep the tips and axes unchanged, so they work for the last step of the L4E (Last 4 Edges) or L3E (Last 3 Edges) method.
Each case states how many edges move and how many are flipped in place. Work out which edges are wrong and pick the matching algorithm.
d.skewb.notation:
A Skewb is a cube cut through the center, with 4 turning axes along the diagonal corners; each turn is 120° and moves half of the puzzle.
The letters are the names of the corners that turn: R (bottom-right-front), L (top-left-front), U (top-right-back), B (bottom-left-back). Clockwise is taken when looking straight at that corner; an apostrophe (') = counterclockwise.
d.skewb.corners:
Sarah's method: these algorithms only permute or twist corners and leave the 6 centers alone. Use them when the centers are right but some corners are in the wrong place or wrongly oriented.
Each case says how many corners move and how many twist in place. Work out which corners are wrong and pick the matching algorithm.
d.skewb.centers:
These algorithms only permute the centers and leave the 8 corners alone. Use them when the corners are right but the centers are mixed up: a 4-center permutation or a 3-center permutation.
Work out which centers are in the wrong places, then run the matching algorithm.

help.title: How to use
help.s1b: Tap the puzzle button at the top left (or pick from the side panel on a tablet) to switch between 3×3, 2×2, 4×4, 5×5, Pyraminx and Skewb.
help.s2b: Pick a level and a set, then tap an algorithm. Use play, pause, step back/forward and restart under the cube; the highlighted move is the one being turned.
help.s3b: Tap “Random case”, solve it yourself, and use “Hide algorithm” to recall it from memory. Each round covers every case before repeating.
help.s4b: Press “Scramble”; the timer starts on your first move and stops when solved. Drag a sticker to turn a layer, drag the background to rotate the view, pinch to zoom. Undo and Redo are unlimited.
help.s5b: You earn 1 exp for every second in the app. Lv 10 unlocks Practice and Play, Lv 15 the advanced levels, Lv 20 the 3×3 Competition sets. Tap the level badge to see your progress.
help.s6b: Tap the ? button on the cube to see what each color and letter means for the current puzzle.
help.s7b: Open the menu at the top right: Sound (background music, turn sound, track), How to use, Appearance (light or dark) and Language.
